extracted.intended_audience: short story writers, magazine editors, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial selection criteria used by an anthology editor to evaluate American short stories (Oct 1919–Sep 1920). Focuses on tests of substance and form, sincerity, presentation, and rules for inclusion in an annual 'best stories' volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of Substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The first test of a short story is 'to report upon how vitally compelling the writer makes his selected facts or incidents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance is achieved by the artist's power of compelling imaginative persuasion which transforms a fact or group of facts into a living truth. The editor calls this the 'test of substance' and uses it as the primary qualitative test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of Form
rubrics_metrics.description: The second test asks whether the artist 'seeks to shape this living substance into the most beautiful and satisfying form, by skilful selection and arrangement of his materials, and by the most direct and appealing presentation of it in portrayal and characterization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form includes selection and arrangement of materials and the directness/appeal of portrayal and characterization; a story that survives both substance and form takes rank above others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic Substance (vs. Inorganic Fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only 'organic substance' — 'substance in which the pulse of life is beating' — is of importance; 'inorganic fiction has been our curse in the past.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for material that feels alive and internally vital; avoid stories where substance is inert or merely decorative. Organic substance means the material is made alive by imaginative transformation, not merely reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological and Imaginative Reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should confer 'psychological and imaginative reality' — a 'fresh, living current which flows through the best of our work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the narrative presents convincing inner life and imaginative truth; this quality is central to the editor's selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / Earnestness of Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor seeks writers 'with something to say' who are 'as much in earnest as a sincere clergyman, an unselfish physician, or an idealistic lawyer.' He emphasizes a 'fight for sincerity' in the short story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value authenticity and seriousness of purpose; prefer writers who truly mean what they say. Anti-patterns include authors who are merely professional, commercial, or performative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Formula and Organized Dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor states 'I am not at all interested in formulae, and organised criticism at its best would be nothing more than dead criticism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject formulaic or dogmatic approaches; prefer fresh, spontaneous artistic discrimination rather than reliance on established tricks or formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and Appealing Presentation (Portrayal and Characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should present substance 'by the most direct and appealing presentation of it in portrayal and characterization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge clarity and emotional appeal in how characters and situations are rendered — directness that makes the material accessible and affecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilful Selection and Arrangement of Materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Form requires 'skilful selection and arrangement of his materials' to shape substance into beautiful and satisfying form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the author's editorial choices: what is included or omitted, narrative order, pacing, and structural unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survivability / Second-Reading Worth
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher distinction is given to narratives 'which may lay convincing claim to a second reading, because each of them has survived both tests, the test of substance and the test of form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that reward re-reading are especially valued; survivability under rereading is a mark of deeper artistic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by Asterisk System
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are grouped by performance: no asterisk = fail to survive either test; one asterisk = survives either substance or form; two asterisks = survives both tests; three asterisks = highest distinction (unites substance and form with such sincerity that they may claim a place in literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit scoring/annotation system used in the yearbook index to indicate relative distinction and to select reprints (stories with triple asterisks are included in the Roll of Honor and reprinted). A personal-preference asterisk may also be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roll of Honor / Highest Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A small group of stories 'possess... the distinction of uniting genuine substance and artistic form in a closely woven pattern with such sincerity' that they may claim a position in literature and are listed in the 'Roll of Honor' (indicated by three asterisks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are considered the most republication-worthy pieces; editor notes the selection does not necessarily mean they are 'great stories' but that they equal roughly five volumes in aggregate worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial Inclusion Rules (American authors only; no translations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor made it 'a point of honor' not to republish an English story nor a translation from a foreign author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection restricted to American-authored stories; translations and English (non‑American) stories are excluded from reprint consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: One Story per Author Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor made it a rule 'not to include more than one story by an individual author in the volume.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits diversity of authors represented; prevents multiple entries by any one author in the anthology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and Non-Ranking (Alphabetical Order)
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of stories in the volume 'is not intended as an indication of their comparative excellence; the arrangement is alphabetical by authors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer ranking from print order; editorial transparency about organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for Writers with a Message / Authentic Perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor seeks 'the man and woman with something to say' who 'see just a little bit more... and who wishes to devote his life to telling us about it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize authors who offer distinct insight or vision rather than cleverness alone; evaluate whether the writer reveals a personal, perceivable vision of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Diverse, Humble Social Voices
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor praises inclusion of diverse racial and social traditions and asks 'Why are we not more curious about the ragman's story and that of the boot-black and the man who keeps the fruit store?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to stories that depict humble or immigrant lives with authenticity; diversity of social experience enriches a national literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Commercialization and Repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor criticizes excessive commercialization and repetition by authors ('the short story was exploited... the magazines which bought and sold fiction like soap'), and warns that 'sloppy sentimentality and slapstick farce ought to bore us frightfully.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disfavor stories produced to formula or commercial fashion; prefer original, earnest work rather than recycled or sensationalist pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Reader Psychology and Magazine Audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor emphasizes understanding 'the psychology of the American reader' and notes that differences between magazine audiences are often artificial and one of emphasis rather than type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a story's qualities will hold the interest of various magazine readerships; universality and sympathetic interpretation of human nature make a story appeal across audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency About Selection Period and Scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection covers stories published in American magazines between October 1919 and September 1920 inclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines the temporal and publication-scope boundary for consideration; any evaluation or comparison should respect this window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for Personal Preference (annotated asterisk)
rubrics_metrics.description: To the titles of certain stories in the 'Rolls of Honor' an asterisk is prefixed revealing 'in some measure a personal preference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor acknowledges subjective tastes can influence final choices; personal-preference markers are explicitly noted.
